utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marro, we are ready to continue. Would you bring in Mr. Prpos?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I just noticed that there is reference to the time served on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I do not see that in the documents. There was some reference to it being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the witness to deal with that matter. The book we have deals with point Orlovci, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I thought so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He mentioned a number of other points which included the bridge, but we have not quite tied that point up. It does only affect two days from the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. DJURO PRPOS, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, were you able to bring with you Exhibits 63, 64, 65, 66, 75 and 77, at least the documents that constitute those Exhibits in their complete form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not managed to do that, but I have conveyed the request to Mr. Mile Jankovic who is responsible. I spoke to him on the phone and I met with him this morning. It is now up to him to try to provide what is necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prpos. Mr. Kay, is it possible for you to speak with that gentleman and tell him that the Trial Chamber has requested the complete documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, these requests have already been made by the Defence in Banja Luka. I have spoken to Professor Wladimiroff this morning. The information I have been given is that it has to go beyond Mr. Jankovic to a higher authority. Quite what that authority is, we do not know and have not been told. But there seems to be a note of optimism that the records will be provided later on in the day. I know that Mr. Keegan has spoken to the Prosecution team about this matter, as I believe he has also been party to the negotiations, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will see then if we are able to get other than what the individual wants us to have. That is our desire to get the complete documents. OK. Fine. You will report back to me and I suppose, Miss Hollis, if you have been in touch with Mr. Keegan, then you will have some input regarding that effort as well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Another possibility for that could be to convey the request to Mr. Neskovic who, I believe, is the deputy Minister of Justice and we have made other requests for information through our officials to him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I understand that both the Prosecution and the Defence have faced difficulties in terms of access to witnesses and documents. So, we will do what we can do to get the documents. A letter or a summons, a subpoena of some sort, would that help?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I think that would be helpful if we are going to deal with Mr. Neskovic or anyone below him, your Honour. They have specifically told us that the procedure they want is something in writing to them, specifying what is being requested.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. If you will then file a motion to that effect requesting the Trial Chamber to make the request and indicate to whom the request should be directed and whether it should be in the form of a summons, and what is requested, then it will be easier for us to proceed. You have no objection, Mr. Kay, to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. Thank you. Miss Hollis, you may continue cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Cross-examined by MISS HOLLIS, continued.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, Mile Jankovic, what is his current position with the opstina Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is Commander of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is Mile his nickname or is that his proper first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is Mr. Jankovic's ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he hold any position in the opstina Prijedor police department in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did he join the opstina Prijedor police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the take over of authority in 1992. He was later my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So in 1992 after the takeover he was your deputy in the traffic section of opstina Prijedor police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere in August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, yesterday I asked you whether in 1992 you had known a soldier named Zoran Karlica. I am afraid because of my poor pronunciation that name may have been translated to you as Zoran Karajica. So I would like to repeat the question to you. In 1992 did you know a soldier named Zoran Karlica which is spelled K-A-R-L-I-C-A ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of him, but I did not know him personally, with that surname, a man with that name.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you, to your knowledge, would not have had any meetings with him in the spring of 1992 prior to the Serb takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday you were talking about reserve policemen who were serving duty in the summer of 1992. You testified that all reserve policemen were performing their duties under a mobilization that had taken place before the conflict. When did that mobilization take place that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mobilization of the reserve police was carried out long before the conflict, while the Ministry for the Internal Affairs at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still operating. At that time the reserve force included members of Muslim ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So what would have been the month and year of this mobilization, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but it was in 1991 that the mobilization was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was this a general mobilization in about September 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not a general mobilization, but only due to increased requirements of the service, the reserve militia (as it was called at the time) was mobilized.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The area of Omarska is part of opstina Prijedor, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in the immediate vicinity there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the period May to December of 1992, did you have any traffic police locations there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except for the checkpoints that I have already listed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were some of those checkpoints close to the Omarska village and area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the closest one was the checkpoint at Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the period May to December 1992, did any of your traffic policemen come from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not one of them, from Omarska, not one.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about the documents that you were shown yesterday. You were shown Defence Exhibits 63, 64 and 65, which were timetables of shifts for June, July and August. I believe you testified that you yourself did not fill in the information on those timetables, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, that is not my job. It is the job of the policemen who is -- whose responsibility it is, but he did so entering information on the basis of a timetable of duty that I authorised.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The gentleman you are referring to is Zoran Cvijic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zoran Cvijic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Would you be present when he actually compiled these documents, these timetables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not present, but I found time to check them out occasionally, and at the end the list is concluded.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Zoran Cvijic's duties kept him in the office most of the time, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, yes, he spent most of his time in the office. That is his job.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were also shown Defence Exhibit 66 which was the official duty plan. Again I believe that you yourself did not make the entries in that duty plan, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would fill in the duty plan at the beginning because, as you can see, this existed all along from 1991. While I was the deputy, I filled it in personally, but later because of my greater responsibilities, then Cvijic filled it in under my supervision, of course.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For the dates, 15 June, 16, 17, 18, 19 June, 2 August, 3 August, it was Zoran Cvijic who filled those entries in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: For the dates between 19th ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to clarify this point. After that duty plan there was another timetable that was typewritten which was certified by my signature, exhibited on the billboard for the policemen to be able to see and only then was it considered final.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This final timetable no longer exists, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, it does not exist in the station.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These timetables that we spoke of, Defence Exhibits 63, 64 and 65, did you keep the originals of those timetables in your personal custody from the time they were created until the present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the original still exists, this book of schedules from 1991, this book is in existence, and there is a list which is a permanent document which has to be kept permanently, though the other document need not necessarily be preserved, but it has been preserved.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But did you yourself keep these documents in your own custody during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The documents are kept in a safe in the station, and policeman Cvijic Zoran is responsible for keeping custody of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 66, is that a document which is also maintained at the police department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please explain which document you are referring to? If you are talking about the payments of personal incomes, then I can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, I was talking about Defence Exhibit 66 which is the official duty plan. Did you keep that document in ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you keep that document in your personal custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I personally do not keep it in custody. I have just said that it is in a safe kept by the policeman responsible for keeping records.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were also shown two pages that were marked "Defence Exhibit 75", and these two pages had to do with a list of reserve policemen. I believe you indicated you did not prepare those two pages, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I do not quite understand which documents you are referring to. If it is a list of workers for whom payment of income is due, then I know what I am being asked.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could ask, please, that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 75?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the Exhibit in front of me. It is a list of members of the reserve police in June and it refers to the payment of personal incomes for that month. The document was written in the station and it bears my signature, typed, typewritten, but as I was absent at that moment it was signed by my superior. It is the first document.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Look at the second page as well and my question is, did you prepare either of these two pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did prepare the second page and it bears my original signature.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said that the first page was written in the station of which I was the Commander, but it was signed by my superior who was the only one authorised to sign it. It refers simply to the payment of personal incomes for policemen, and because I was absent and it was urgent he signed it on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The second page that has your signature, did you yourself actually type that information in that page or did you sign the document after someone else prepared it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just signed it. The typing is done by the typist working in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You were also shown Defence Exhibit 77 which you, I believe, indicated was a document that would have come from the accounting department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a joint document with a list of members of all policemen in the public security station. This can be seen from this RSM. This is the station of the reserve force from 130 to 139, and the numbers above in which Dusko Tadic is included is a list of my station. This is from the accounting service of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So each of these RSMs indicate different stations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. This should not confuse you -- I beg your pardon -- because this list and the previous lists are prepared in the accounting department, but the payment of salaries is carried out on the basis of signatures. Every station has to provide a list to the accounting department and then the accounting department draws up this kind of list.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you present when Defence Exhibit 77 was prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present when this Exhibit was prepared as this list is not part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you keep the original of this list in your personal custody from the time it was created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All documents are kept in a safe of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us if there is any significance to the numbers that appear in column 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes. You see that there are numbers beginning with 116 and going numerically down the page; do you know if there is any significance to those numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is simply a series of names of policemen figuring on the joint list. Dusko Tadic is under the number 128. The numbers above him belong to the traffic police station. The numbers from 130 refer to one of the police stations covered by the public security department which included several stations. This is the list comprising all members receiving salaries, because the accounting is common for the entire public security service.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know why some of those numbers are circled, for example, 116, 117, 127? Do you know why those circles are around those particular numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that policemen could come to pick up their salaries personally to the accounting department, and then the responsible accountant encircled the number to know that somebody had already picked up his salary; or there were cases that a policeman working on the records would pick up the whole sum of salaries for the whole station and he would sign that he had picked up the salary for all his workers. So that I assume that this encircling meant that people, these particular people, had picked up their salaries in the accounting department itself.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The column 5 on this form, can you tell us what information would go in column 5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell with certainty because I do not have the beginning, the first page, but perhaps if I could look at this record from the police station?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you are looking at, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One might say that No. 1 is the number, second, name, third, where he worked, (4) number of days, (5) work organisations, (6) amount and (7) signature, if we look at document No. 2 with the headings of the columns.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you talking about Defence Exhibit 75, the listing of members of the reserve police? Is that the document you are looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that document can also be used, but on that document there is no column to indicate where the policemen were working, because some of those reserve policemen were employed, but they responded to the obligation of mobilization and they worked as traffic policemen. This information can be found on document No. 2.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prpos. Can you tell us, please, what was the distance from the Orlovci checkpoint to the Omarska detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the Omarska crossroads, the distance from Prijedor is 25 kilometres or, rather, 22 and a half, and to Orlovci, four to five kilometres. So that makes it 17, and from the crossroads to Omarska, three, and that makes it about 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So from Orlovci checkpoint to the detention camp at Omarska was about 20 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly about 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever drive from the Orlovci checkpoint to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did on one occasion when a deputy of the Republika Srpska, Vojo Kupresanin, took his colleague, a Muslim -- I cannot recollect the name of that deputy -- he took him out of the camp and to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When was this that you went to the Omarska detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the exact date, but on that particular occasion I accompanied deputy Kupresanin to the camp, and when he took over the deputy of Muslim ethnicity, I accompanied them to the crossroads of the main road from where they went on to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what month it was that you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recollect just now what month it was; I just know that it was the one occasion I went there and never again. I just remembered the name -- Semenovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp who met you at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went as far as the gate and then I did not go any further.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of the guards at the gate when you arrived at the gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember any one of them now.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You cannot remember them or you did not know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew them by sight, but I am not very good at names, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I believe you indicated that the man who was taken from the camp was Semenovic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who else was in this delegation that went to the camp on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just the driver and the deputy, Vojo Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the driver's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have a driver that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I drove personally.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What vehicle did you drive there? What type of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a police vehicle which I drove usually myself at that time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It is one of the white and blue police vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, blue and white with the alarm signals on it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that a Golf type vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Concerning your visits to the checkpoints, were there not some days that you were too busy to go to all of the checkpoints for each shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my only task ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, I do not recall, would you ask the witness how many checkpoints were under his direction? I do not remember. I also had some questions about Defence 75, but I will ask him at some point.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, can you hear me again? We cannot hear you, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you fine.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good. Now we can hear you as well.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, how many checkpoints were you responsible for in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For four checkpoints, Orlovci, Crna Dolina, Trinaesta and Most Na Sani.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you went to these checkpoints, how long would you remain at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on necessity, half an hour, an hour, depending on the subject matter involved at the checkpoint, and I tried to be with policemen as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On 17th June, can you tell us which checkpoint you visited first on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really would not know, because I wanted to have a surprise factor involved and to check on the policemen so I would always change their turns. So sometimes I would go direct, sometimes I would make an entire circle. I would change the time when I would come in so the policemen never knew when I would come at what time and in which order.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, can you remember the time that you arrived at the first checkpoint on 17th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you remember how long you stayed at that first checkpoint on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is impossible to remember now after all this time, and the situation was such in those days, and there were so many things to do, and I really cannot remember all of that now.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you would not remember what time it was you went to Dule Tadic's checkpoint when he was on duty on 17th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not remember.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you would have stayed at his checkpoint when you went there on 17th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about your activities during the time period May to December 1992. During that time were you involved in any Serb attacks on non-Serb towns or villages in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you involved in the takeover of any non-Serb towns or villages in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I want to say now you asked me last time whether I knew that takeover of power was being prepared. I said that I did not know, because my first wife is of Croat nationality and I have two children with her. Regrettably, she died in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, you knew about the plan for the takeover in opstina Prijedor and you participated in this planning and you benefited from it, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know until that moment before the immediate takeover -- that is exactly what I told you yesterday -- but immediately I decided what side I would take because my neighbours, Croats and Muslims, opened my eyes and I had no dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: I have asked you about whether you were involved in Serb attacks and takeovers of villages in opstina Prijedor. Were you aware of such attacks and takeovers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not participate in that nor did I know about such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you take part in any looting of non-Serb property in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can be assured by the property I have now, that is a Lada vehicle, car, of 1977.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that such looting was occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it, like in any war that was present too.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw it how did you react to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within the scope of my possibilities and authority, I tried to prevent it, and that was the function of the checkpoints that were established.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The people who were doing this looting, did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: This looting that you saw, where was it occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like everywhere in the zones where there were war operations.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the specific locations where you saw people looting? Was it in the town of Prijedor? Was it in the village of Orlovci? Do you recall those locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such things, wherever property is not under control, looting happens under normal conditions, let alone in the chaos that occurred then.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you saw this looting what was being stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly vehicles that we would then take at the checkpoint when we would check these vehicles. This was the task of the policemen. If vehicles were driven by people who were not their owners, they were taken away from them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So if a person came to a checkpoint, was driving a vehicle he did not own, that vehicle was immediately taken from him, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if he could not prove the origin of the vehicle, perhaps he had purchased the vehicle earlier and he did not manage to transfer it into his own name yet. So such vehicles were taken away and then through appropriate proceedings, if he managed to prove that it was his vehicle, then the vehicle would be returned to that person.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this same time period I was talking about, May to December 1992, did you take part in any killings or beatings of non-Serb civilians in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wish to say here that my competences are quite clear. My authority was to control traffic in the area of Prijedor, and I and my policemen did not do anything beyond that, that is to say, to ensure that traffic takes place in an unhindered manner and that we exercise control over participants in traffic as well as over freight that was being transported in that traffic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that such beatings and killings were occurring, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In fact, was the Prijedor police department not extensively involved in setting up and guarding camps that were established in the opstina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but that was under the authority of others, not within my scope of authority.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Prijedor police department was involved in rounding up people and taking them to the camps, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to ask the heads of those police departments. I am responsible for the things I did and the policemen whose Commander I was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that your responsibilities were to control traffic, to control the roads, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: As head of the traffic section, you must have been involved in meetings with other section heads and higher authorities in the police department, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such co-ordination has to exist. There is a leader who co-ordinates all these activities.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These meetings would have been held on a regular basis, would they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on possibilities, because the situation was such that sometimes there could not be meetings because of all these things that were happening and the blockade that we were in until the corridor was established. You can understand the situation that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Which corridor are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corridor towards mainstream Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mean the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These meetings that ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we were ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- you attended, at these meetings issues that were relevant to the police would have been discussed, would they not, issues and problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You indicated that these meetings were for co-ordination so information would have been shared when it would have impacted other sections, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you would have been told about events that would affect traffic flow and checkpoints, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for what I was responsible, that is to say, primarily ensuring a normal flow of traffic and the functioning of normal city life, and control over the observance of regulations, traffic regulations, that were taken over from the former Yugoslavia, and we act in accordance with them until the present day, as far as traffic is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you would have been told when bus loads of prisoners were being taken from camp to camp, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You would have been told when convoys of Muslims were being forcibly removed from the opstina, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not forcibly removed. They went of their own free will. I am trying to say that a long time before the war a lot of Muslims removed their families from there, including the Commander with whom I exchanged apartments at his initiative because he was alone in a three room apartment and I with five family members was in a two room apartment. So a lot before these events took place, they shipped their families out of Prijedor, which is to say that they knew what would happen during the war. Even when they went then, they went voluntarily because they applied to the Red Cross and they went in that way, not forcibly.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Prpos, is it your testimony that the thousands of Muslims who left opstina Prijedor between May and December 1992 did so purely voluntarily? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, and also what I said that many people went before the war voluntarily because living conditions were such that whoever had any possibility to leave actually did leave, because it is only a few days ago that we got a regular supply of electricity, not to speak of other normal needs of any person.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In your position, as head of the traffic section, between May and December 1992, you would have been alerted to the daily movement of interrogators to Omarska and other camps, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went through the Orlovci checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you were aware of those movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was, and the policemen at the checkpoint did.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You would have been told when bus loads of prisoners from cleansed Muslims villages were being taken to camps, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what kind of cleansing you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When the Muslims were forced to leave their homes and taken in buses to camps, you would have been told about those bus loads who were traversing your roads, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Policemen at the checkpoint knew about such cases, but I repeat again, it was not a question of forcible removal. This was organised by the Prijedor Red Cross, and the police only provided safe passage to these convoys which is a normal thing to do for policemen from any police station.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was it the Red Cross who organised the camp at Omarska and the camp at Keraterm? These were Red Cross camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but I do not think that the Red Cross did that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: All of these movements on the roads in opstina Prijedor, you would have been told about those movements ahead of time, would you not, so you could alert your personnel about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, policemen at checkpoints had strict instructions what their task was to do at checkpoints, that is to say, they had certain instructions, and normally when they would stop a vehicle they would assure themselves of what was going on, and then these vehicles would continue their travel or they would be detained there depending on the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Some of these buses that were taking people from villages came to the SUP at which you worked, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, buses did not come to SUP. Even if they did come there, I cannot claim that because my job was not directly linked to SUP only because I had to work on the ground and go to different places.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: But you were certainly at the SUP from time to time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In fact, when buses came to the SUP some Muslim prisoners were taken off those buses at the SUP, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I am not aware of such buses coming to SUP. I do not know about it, but I do not preclude the possibility of them having come there while I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you do not recall any occasion when you were at the SUP and prisoners were brought there and beaten at the SUP, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You do not recall any occasion, for example, between 24th and 28th May 1992, when you were at the SUP and saw prisoners come to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You do not recall any occasions, say, between 24th and 28th May 1992, when after these prisoners were brought to the SUP you heard their screams and cries as they were beaten there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You are not aware of any of that type of activity, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, I have a few questions for you in re-examination: you were asked about the salary documents. Do you recollect that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They have been given a label in Court as D74, 75 and 77. First of all, if D74 can be put in front of you -- sorry, D75 actually. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, it will be Defence Exhibit 75, two pages, and then Defence Exhibit 77, one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It is the salary list of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have that list in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were asked whether this document would remain within your custody. In your duties as a police officer over the last 20 years, would it be possible for you to keep all the documents that you had ever been involved with actually within your physical custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is never possible, because the very fact that after changing the duty I am actually involved in, I do not have access to the records that are in the traffic department of the police station. That is to say, that all archives have to be kept in the safe of that police station, depending on the period involved. So not a single policeman can personally take that home. This is kept in a safe and everyone is responsible for a certain part of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, does the police station then have a system for keeping documents that are created during the administration of the police station so that they are kept in a safe place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are exact instructions from the Ministry of the Interior for every document. It says how it is to be kept safe, and there is also a list of lasting, durable goods that have to be kept in a station. So these lists and schedules are of a periodical nature though, so they do not have to be kept permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document that we are looking at as D75, is there any reason to believe that it is unusual or not created properly in the usual course of the administration of the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no doubt because it is only natural that a typist would type this out on the basis of the records that are kept in the police station, and it is signed by the head of that station and also there is a seal affixed to it, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the same question about the second page of D75, that is the next document. Again, is there anything about this document that makes you think that it is unusual or different from what the document should be if created in the usual course of administration of that police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no difference and there is nothing strange about it. This document has my original signature though, and perhaps it may be a bit misleading that on this first paper it was signed by my superior because probably I was away, and because of the urgency of having salaries paid out he signed the document instead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at the other salary Exhibit, D77, if that could be placed in front of you? That is the document with the figure "4" at the top of the page. I will ask the same question about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there anything unusual about this document ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- that makes you believe that it was not ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- there is nothing unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the typist. I mean, do you know who the typist would be for any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that it was Anka and I cannot remember her surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did she have a job as a typist to type down the information that was given to her on the forms that we have seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she was the typist in the station, and she was engaged because she had already retired before that, but she had been working as a typist for a long time. So she was called back to work at the station because there was a shortage of typists. Before that, there was a Muslim lady, Nadzija, who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you had any complaints of forgery by Zoran Cvijic who created the schedule and wrote on the official duty plan? Have there ever been any complaints that he has made up any of the entries within those books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never, especially with these lists of salaries that you asked me about, you know that workers are the most sensitive in that respect. So, as far as these lists are concerned and any other documents that were processed by Zoran Cvijic, there were never any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us why it is that Zoran Cvijic will not give evidence to the Tribunal here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to that. That is certainly going to be speculative on this witness's part.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, excuse me one minute, would you take your earphones off, please? Yes, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We are going to object to that certainly in the form that it is asked. It is not based on hearsay but at this point in time it appears it would be purely speculative on this witness's part. There is no indication that the other witness or the other person has talked with him and passed on this information.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, if the proper foundation is laid then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can answer this question because ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rather than you answering it, do you want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will ask if he has spoken to her.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could put your headphones back on, please, Mr. Prpos?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to Mr. Zoran Cvijic about his reasons why he will not give evidence before the Tribunal at the Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have during my contacts with the Defence when they were coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of him being asked to give evidence either before the Judges in The Hague in person or by video link from Banja Luka to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and as far as I know he said resolutely that he did not want to appear either in Banja Luka or in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he requested on one occasion or more than one occasion to give evidence in some form before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions he was requested and I personally tried to convince him of that, but he was categorical, and I did not want -- I do not want to be the judge of that, why he does not want to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he give an explanation to you as to particular problems that he suffered from which caused him not to want to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that he justified that by health conditions. He thought that he was unable to stand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you aware if he has had any psychiatric problems that excused him from any part of his mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, all the time he was in the station and he fulfilled his duties in terms of mobilization. He did have some trouble in terms of nervousness, like any normal person during the time of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you think you will be able to ask him again whether he will co-operate and give evidence before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could, but I said that already on several occasions I tried to convince him to do so, but he was categorical about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for dealing with that matter. You mentioned amongst the checkpoints that came under the traffic security one at the Sani. Is that at a bridge over the Sana River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: While you are asking these questions ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- if he could use Prosecution Exhibit 280 and point out the locations of the four checkpoints, I would appreciate that. I wanted to ask him and now is a good point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, the book we looked at that contained the checkpoint Orlovci duty rosters, would that also have contained in a separate part of the page the list of those who would have been present for duty at the Sana River on, for instance, 2nd or 3rd August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, each checkpoint had a number and it was on a unified list for that day. In addition to activities at the checkpoint, on the schedule there were other activities of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You have now got Exhibit 280 in front of you. At the request of the Court, I would like you to indicate to us where the checkpoints were located by your traffic security police. First of all, if you could identify where checkpoint Orlovci was situated and if the camera can focus on to the particular part of the map that you can point us to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated]. The checkpoint Orlovci is on the part of the Prijedor to Banja Luka main road, about four or five kilometres from Prijedor. It is roughly here. [The witness indicated]. It is about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can the monitor be taken back a bit or moved across so that we can see where the pointer is on the map? If you could put your pointer back to the place on the map and hold it there for 10 seconds at the point of checkpoint Orlovci? Could we focus in on where the pointer is on the map? If we can go close into the pointer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can the monitor be taken into where the red biro is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We can see.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think that will be the best we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I know your Honours were concerned as to the mixture of the roads at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can ask him if it is on the main road. That might resolve that. The others we have not seen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see the point 83 and where the roads are. Thank you very much, Mr. Prpos. If the monitor can be taken back? If you could indicate to us the positions of the other checkpoints around Prijedor that were under your control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next checkpoint is the Crna Dolina or Black Valley checkpoint on a part of the main road in the direction of Kozarska Dubica. It is somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you keep your pen on the spot so that we can see exactly? Near that point of 183 -- 163, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could show us the site of the next checkpoint? Perhaps the monitor can come back again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next checkpoint is the so-called Trinaesta or the Thirteenth on the main road Prijedor to Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one moment. Is it on the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the next checkpoint was the bridge on the Sana.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us go back. Is it on the yellow road there or the red road?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is the checkpoint point on the way to Bosanski Novi, I think it was, Bosanski Novi is that road, on the main road, on the red road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the main road, at the crossroads with the yellow road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could be so kind to show us again where the checkpoint is for the Sana River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the bridge linking the main road from Prijedor to Sanski Most crossing the Sana River here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would also like to say that there was a checkpoint at Gomjenica on the road from Prijedor to Tomasica. It is also on the Gomjenica river which flows into the Sana here. This checkpoint functioned occasionally from time to time depending on circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again is that on the red road on the map across the other side of the river from Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the red road. It is in the direction of Gomjenica. The settlement is called Gomjenica, and it is this bridge here where the river Gomjenica flows into the River Sana.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that deal with the matters for your Honours?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is all I ask and I note the time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, one question: after you had on your daily checks of whether or not your police were vigilant and in attention at the checkpoints, after you had made one visit to a checkpoint, were the police there confident that you would not appear again that day or did you sometimes make two visits? In other words, having been there once, could they be confident that you would not return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they could not be confident that I would not return because I said at the beginning I changed the times. I chose different times in order to surprise them so that they would never know from what direction I would come to check on them. There were cases that I would visit a certain checkpoint three times in one day, depending on my assessment, whether it was necessary to check on the quality of the work of the policemen there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that anyway is the purpose of a control service.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, would you ask that Defence 75 be placed in front of you and 77, the accounting sheets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the documents in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Before I ask you about those, let me ask you about the four checkpoints under your control. Were they manned 24 hours a day? Mr. Prpos, we lost contact with you. So my question is were those checkpoints, the four checkpoints under your control, manned 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all 24 hours. There was duty and the shifts were replaced at the checkpoint itself.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you made these visits, I gather you never found that a police officer was not on duty, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my tours there were never such cases.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Defence 75, the first page, you have explained the columns on that page. At the bottom, next to Mr. Tadic's name, on the first page of 75, there is a number 16. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, it says "16-30."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means -- it means that he worked from 16th June to 30th June, a total of 13 days. It means he started working on 16th in the police station for traffic security, and since a month has 30 days, that gives you the number 13.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Are these forms supposed to indicate the number of days that a person worked at the Orlovci checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily for Orlovci only. This list shows how many policemen worked in that particular month because on the basis of these lists they were paid incomes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But if ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, if we divide the amount with the number of days, we get what the remuneration was for one day.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But these lists would indicate the officers who worked at one of the four checkpoints under your control, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only at the checkpoints. For instance, in the particular case of Dusko Tadic, it was just the Orlovci checkpoint, but it applies to all the duties of policemen during the month. A policeman may be working at other places, not necessarily at checkpoints. He may have had other duties.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you have any control over the Kozarac police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So time spent at the Kozarac police station would not be reflected on these Exhibits 75 and 77, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular case of this list which belonged to the traffic security police station, but the other list, No. 3, in the public security station, there you have a list including policemen from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. I was just talking about Exhibits 75 and 77. This is for time spent under your control, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It applies exclusively to members of the police force in my station.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then on the same page there is a number adjacent to that. What is that number? A dinar amount?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the salary the person received for that part of the month.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How much is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can see, 3,700.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is that based on the number of days worked that month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the No. 13, that is how this sum was calculated.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then turn to the next page of Exhibit 75. You see line 8, "Tadic Dusko"? Is this for July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is this for July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably, but you cannot see the heading here, not even the name of the police station of the traffic police. In the process of copying it was probably missed out, but probably it applies to July.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Next to Mr. Tadic's name, at least on my copy, the number of days and the dates served are blocked out. Is it on your copy as well?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: On the next page of 75 which you believe is July, is there an indication of the number of days worked and the dates worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is, only during copying probably the person above him spent the same time working as he did, so that this is just confirmed in the case of Dusko Tadic. There is a ditto sign, so this is for the month of July. You can see compared to the amount, if we compare this amount with the previous amount, then we can see how many days. Here it is 9,300 and for 13 days he got 3,700.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So then Mr. Tadic worked the number of days that the person above him worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, the same number of days of the person above him or maybe even two persons above him on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was the rate per day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a daily rate, but at the end of the month or sometimes it was -- the payments were delayed by two or three months. It depended on the resources available at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So there was no set amount that a police officer was paid per day or per month or per week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was determined after the month expired. I told you, when the funds came in and then we could pay out personal incomes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How did you determine how much to pay out to a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was determined by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska. There was a uniform rate for all policemen in Republika Srpska. You can see that the list that we would send from the police stations does not contain that sum. The sum was determined in the accountancy department itself.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was that determined on a daily basis, on the number of days a person worked or a weekly basis or a monthly rate, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was determined on a daily basis, but this daily sum varied from one month to another because of the differences in the funds available in the Ministry, as I mentioned. So that the salary was calculated on the basis of the number of days worked but there was no fixed rate.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. On the last page 77, Defence 77, would this ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: --- reflect the number of days that Mr. Tadic worked at the Orlovci checkpoint in August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at the Orlovci checkpoint, but for that month. He left my station on August 3rd. So this is a unified list on the basis of which personal income was paid to Dusko Tadic and that is 26 days in that month, including the three days he worked in my station and in the other stations to which he was transferred. This is a unified list of the accounting department where all lists provided by individual police stations came together and the accounts were made.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is this Defence 77 a different document than Defence 75? It looks different at the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is different in so far that this is a document of a particular police station, and document 77 is the document of the accounting department in the public security centre because, as I said, that public security centre had several police stations under it, and this can be seen from the continuation of this list when you go on to No. 130, it is another police station, then 139, another reserve police station and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So then 75 would reflect that Mr. Tadic worked as a policeman for the Republika Srpska for 26 days from January -- is that correct? I mean, from August 1st to August 31st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, do you recall testifying that at one point Mr. Tadic served on the Sana River checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So all of the time of Mr. Tadic's service under your control he was at the Orlovci checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there is a list and on the last day that he spent in the station there is mention of the bridge on the Sana which is probably an error made after I had left that police station.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where is that indicated? That would be in 63, is it, that is the 66, rather, or perhaps the spreadsheets? I am asking you, Mr. Prpos, for help. Where is that indicated that there was service at the Sana River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a list which was given much earlier on by Commander Mile Jankovic indicating days when he worked, and in one case this last checkpoint of the bridge on the Sana is mentioned, but according to the official documents of duty service and timetables, this cannot be found.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I am asking you to point to me where there is an indication that he served on the Sana River assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have that list, but I saw it early on. We do not have that list here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you had indicated you were going to tie that up. Where does it come from. Maybe we can help Mr. Prpos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was indicating I could not tie that up as it had been something that I had not been able to trace. But I think if your Honour looks at 65A or B, depending upon which is the better copy -- if 65A or B could be put in of in front of the witness -- your Honour can see 1st August, the duty of 7 to 19?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 2nd August, free.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 3rd August, 7 to 19. If your Honour goes to the book D66, 1st August ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- 7 to 19 which reflects the schedule we just looked at; 2nd August, "slobodni", free; 3rd August, not on for point Orlovci which is why I asked ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police station, one can see if he had been in the police station, he would have been listed among those free. So that means that on 3rd August he was not in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could ask a question, your Honour, to the witness ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- because it may be I can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the page that we are looking at for 3rd August, Mr. Prpos -- if you could open it again to 3rd August -- we see point Orlovci. On this page of the book, would there be the point for the Sana River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one would have to indicate all the checkpoints, Most Na Sani, Trinaesta and Crna Dolina. So you see the difference for checkpoints Orlovci from 7 to 19. The other checkpoints would be listed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If he was still under your control on 3rd August but not at point Orlovci but at another checkpoint, could it be that we would find that elsewhere on the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would have to be indicated if he was engaged anywhere in this police station. If he were free, then he would be listed as free as you had occasion to see on other schedules and for other days. Therefore, on August 3rd he was no longer on the list of the police station for traffic security, according to the duty schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you or did you cause to be supplied to the Defence just the readings, though, for point Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, wherever Dusko Tadic's name appears.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think I understand where you are going.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, you indicated that you had seen somewhere, I believe, that Mr. Tadic was assigned to the Sana River checkpoint, but you believe that is a mistake, is that not so or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: OK. But it is possible that there is another sheet that the Defence saw that we do not have in Defence 66A that would indicate that he was assigned somewhere other than Orlovci on August 3rd, because it does indicate on the spreadsheet that he was working, is that correct, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour is putting it right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may look at the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It says here on 3rd August Dusko worked from 7 to 19, and that is the list that was given in the first contact by the police station for traffic security and signed by Mile Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where does this information come from, the information on that spreadsheet you have before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this list during first contacts when I was told that I would be a witness in the case against Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Where did the information come from that is put on that spreadsheet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It comes from the police station for traffic security and signed by Mile Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Does it come from the duty roster book which you were looking at earlier, Defence 66, or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably it comes from the duty roster which is final, but that information was given by Mile Jankovic and not me because I was no longer in that station at the time, on the basis of records which are left in the custody of the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One further question: if, in fact, Dule Tadic left the traffic police on or about 3rd August and went into the ordinary police, his service during that time when he was in the ordinary police would not appear in any of these records that we are looking at, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are records of other police stations. That is the station to which he was transferred. So there must be in the records of that police station when he started working there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, quite, but service in the ordinary police as distinct from the traffic police would not appear on these particular sheets we have been looking at with your help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would not, because these are documents of the police station for traffic security that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, let me just follow up: Defence 77 would pick up the 26 days that Mr. Tadic worked, presumably one two or perhaps three (as soon as we find out what happens to August 3rd) with you and then the rest of the time in Kozarac for a total of 26 days in August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is to be further evidence. Can I just deal with one matter which may make this clear?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. It is clear now, but you may go ahead, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, can you go back to sheet 65B to the "remarks" column, D65B, the sheet for August '92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, I do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The remarks ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have D65B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the "remarks" column of column 7, if you can just read out the remarks there against Dusko Tadic's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Remarks" are there, yes. I apologise. I have the text in English here. I need the Serbian. I have the document D65A with the text in Serbian. Under "remarks" it says that -- the copy is not parallel with the line, but if I go from the bottom it is No. 3 and it says: "On 5th August '92 he was transferred to the reserve police station centre 1 because of the needs of the service", and my signature stands there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could tell us what reserve police centre 1 is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the reserve police station centre 1. It is one of the reserve police stations within the centre for public security of Prijedor, among which was the police station for traffic security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If that indicates he was transferred there on 5th August and continued working with the reserve police, is that why we would see in the accountancy document his work stretching from 1st August to 31st August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and since the accountancy service is one for all, then it has a single list covering the period from 1st to 31st August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is further evidence to come on this matter, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. 65(B), the English, we had discovered there was an error in the translation. It was August 3rd, we have changed it to August 5th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not recall it, but mine is 5th August quite clearly on the document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then maybe we have entered August 5th. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Serbian document is much clearer, your Honour, than the English.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have additional questions of Mr. Prpos?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I do not, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, earlier I had asked you about whether you participated in certain activities in opstina Prijedor during the period May to December 1992. During the period May to December 1992 and also 1993, were you involved in any thefts of property in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nor did I need that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any complaints against you for thefts of any kind of property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you involved in any kinds of thefts of firewood or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any complaints that you stole firewood during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the witness being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, we do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prpos, you are excused and you are free to go home or to your office at this time. However, you may be recalled as a witness so you should continue to make yourself available to return to testify. You should keep in touch with Mr. Wladimiroff. Mr. Wladimiroff will tell you if you have been asked by the Tribunal to return for testimony. Will you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. I am at your disposal, as necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you, Mr. Prpos. Thank you for coming. You are now excused. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Wladimiroff sitting there not in his robe. Can you see? Lucky, very comfortable! Would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The next witness is Mirko Vujanovic. MIRKO VUJANOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Marro, would you please administer the oath to Mr. Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano?

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Witness, is your name Mirko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Do you live in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MISS DE BERTODANO
utterances.text: Have you always lived in Prijedor?
